name: Feldera
license: MIT for the open-source edition (the Rust crates are published as MIT OR Apache-2.0); since May 2026 the repository also contains Enterprise-only code, behind a `feldera-enterprise` feature flag, that needs a paid licence. The engine began at VMware Research, also under MIT
summary: An incremental view maintenance engine in Rust: you write SQL tables and views, and it keeps every view up to date by processing only the changes, based on the award-winning DBSP theory.
intro: A Feldera pipeline is a SQL program: `CREATE TABLE` statements are the inputs and `CREATE VIEW` statements the outputs, and views can build on views. Feldera’s compiler, written in Java on Apache Calcite, turns the program into a Rust program on DBSP (Database Stream Processor), compiles it and runs it as one process. Connectors attached to each table in a `WITH` clause feed it changes, meaning inserts and deletes (an update is both): Kafka topics, HTTP, Debezium or PostgreSQL CDC, Delta Lake, Iceberg, S3 files, Pub/Sub and others. DBSP represents each batch of changes as a Z-set, rows with a weight of +1 or -1, and computes exactly how every view changes, using indexes it keeps for joins and aggregates; that state can grow larger than memory and spill to disk. The result is the same as rerunning every query in a batch engine, but the work is proportional to the change, not to the data. View changes go out through sink connectors (Kafka, Delta Lake, PostgreSQL, Snowflake, Redis, DynamoDB); Iceberg output goes through Kafka Connect. Feldera keeps a view’s full contents only if it is declared `MATERIALIZED`, and those can be queried ad hoc through Apache DataFusion. `LATENESS` on a timestamp column tells it how late events may arrive, so it can drop state it will never need again.

The open-source edition, free under MIT, runs a pipeline on a single node in a single container, with full SQL and every connector. Feldera Enterprise runs in your Kubernetes cluster with one pod per pipeline and adds checkpoints, fault tolerance and disaster recovery, changing a running program without losing its state, multi-host pipelines (in preview), SSO and role-based access, at custom prices. The engine comes from VMware Research, where Mihai Budiu and Leonid Ryzhyk developed DBSP; their paper won a Best Paper award at VLDB 2023, the year they and three colleagues founded Feldera.
strengths: Evaluates whole SQL programs incrementally, including joins, aggregates, correlated subqueries, window functions, recursive queries and stacks of views, with results that match a batch run on the same input
Work is proportional to the size of each change, so the same SQL can backfill history and then keep up with live data
Built on a peer-reviewed theory: DBSP won a VLDB 2023 Best Paper award, and its maths has been formalised in the Lean theorem prover
A single Rust process with state that can exceed memory, and connectors for Kafka, CDC, Delta Lake, Iceberg, warehouses and databases
limits: The free edition has no checkpoints or fault tolerance: after a crash or restart a pipeline must re-ingest its inputs, and changing a program while keeping its state is Enterprise-only too
Not a database: no transactions or concurrency control, views aren’t stored unless materialized, and applications usually read results from a sink
Every change to the SQL compiles a new Rust program before the pipeline can start; Enterprise offers parallel compilation to speed this up
Licensing is now mixed: the MIT core shares the repository with Enterprise code under Feldera’s terms (GitHub shows the licence as NOASSERTION), and Enterprise prices aren’t published
Some connectors are experimental, such as PostgreSQL CDC and Iceberg input, and recursive queries use Feldera’s own syntax rather than standard SQL

snippet.title: A Feldera program: two input tables, a materialized join, and a view streamed to Kafka
source: ts TIMESTAMP NOT NULL LATENESS INTERVAL 1 HOURS  -- at most an hour out of order
-- filled through the REST API, a file or a CDC connector
customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
-- kept up to date from changes only; a customer moving country updates both rows
SELECT c.country, COUNT(*) AS purchases, SUM(p.amount) AS revenue
FROM purchases p JOIN customers c ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id
-- each change to this view is sent to Kafka as an insert or a delete
AS SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total

Your Kubernetes cluster, cloud or on premises; one pod per pipeline

rows.label: SQL and connectors
values: Full SQL, all connectors, state larger than memory

rows.label: Checkpoints and fault tolerance
values: Checkpoints every 60 seconds by default, at-least-once or exactly-once recovery, sync to S3 for disaster recovery

rows.label: Change the SQL, keep the state
values: No: a modified program starts from scratch
Yes: only new or modified views are recomputed

sections.title: Other engines that keep SQL results fresh

items.name: RisingWave
items.text: A streaming database that speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol and keeps tables, views and internal state in object storage, so applications query materialized views directly. Premium features need a licence key.

items.name: Materialize
items.text: Strongly consistent views over PostgreSQL, MySQL and Kafka sources, queried over the PostgreSQL protocol. Free use is limited to installations under 24 GiB of memory and 48 GiB of disk.

items.name: Flink SQL
items.text: Continuous queries over dynamic tables in Apache Flink, also equivalent to batch results on a snapshot. A distributed framework that writes results to other systems rather than serving them.

story: In 2018 Leonid Ryzhyk and Mihai Budiu at VMware Research started Differential Datalog, a library for computing over continuously changing data. By around 2020 it ran in VMware Skyline’s cloud service for thousands of customers, but watching developers write their rules convinced the team they needed a better experience, and SQL was familiar. Budiu and Ryzhyk went back to the theory and, in 2022, defined DBSP, a small algebra of streams that can turn any query into one that processes only changes, with proofs that the result matches recomputing from scratch.

Their paper with Tej Chajed, Frank McSherry and Val Tannen won a Best Paper award at VLDB 2023. In August 2023 they announced Feldera, the company, with Lalith Suresh, Ben Pfaff and Gerd Zellweger from VMware and seed funding led by Costanoa; the MIT-licensed code moved from VMware to the new company, by then with a SQL compiler built on Apache Calcite and an engine in Rust.

Feldera has since moved from streaming toward replacing batch jobs that rerun over mostly unchanged data. In May 2026 it began keeping Enterprise code in the same repository under separate terms, and in September 2026 it announced $21.5 million in Series A and seed funding led by Inovia Capital.

choices.choice: A theory first, then the engine
choices.why: The team had seen general incremental engines fail through engineering alone. DBSP gives provably correct rules for each operator and a recipe for adding new ones without breaking correctness.
Differential Datalog worked in production, but the team wanted a better developer experience and SQL was familiar and well understood, so DBSP was built to evaluate full SQL, including recursion.
Translating SQL into a specialised Rust program, rather than interpreting a plan, gives native speed and memory safety without a garbage collector.
Feldera guarantees that view contents always equal what a batch system would compute on the same input, so incremental results can replace batch jobs.
